title: 在采集时聚合指标：Reddit 的 Prometheus 物化指标与生产优化
author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
content:
Brief Description

Materialized metrics: scrape-time aggregation in Prometheus - Walther Lee

Table of Contents

  • Materialized metrics and aggregation design
  • Timing accuracy and production issues
  • Demonstration and discussion

Materialized metrics and aggregation design

Hello everybody. Well, yeah, my name is Walter Lee. I'm a software engineer at Reddit. And today we're going to talk about materialized metrics, which is a way of aggregating metrics as scrape time. This is something I've been working at Reddit for the last I think eight or nine months. And we did it in three different fa uh phases. The first one was being able to just do the thing aggregate while we scrape uh do all the ingestion part of materialized metrics. Then we also work on the query side once we had something working on production. How can we use these materialized metrics on the background so that users don't need to change their queries and dashboards um to be able to just use materialized metrics before uh without needing to rename everything. And the last stage was incorporate incorporating materialist metrics with the components that we use which uh credit is Thanos with Prometheus.

So that me that meant connecting materialist metrics with Thanos. But in this case, I only have 20 minutes. So I'm going to be only talking about the ingestion part which I think presented the most challenges and we can hack those 20 minutes. And if you have any questions about the query side, I can also talk about that. Okay. So what's the problem? I think we all are familiar with the issue here. Cardality is paid at query time. You obviously also pay for this cardality when you ingest it. But from the user point of view, you can have exactly the same query. You can be expecting exactly the same number of series in your response but the latency and the processing in the background can be complete different and again from the user point of view many times this difference doesn't make any sense.

Your current can change because you had deployments because there was no rotations and the user is is paying with latency and waiting for that data just because of there was process that they didn't change. The standard way of fixing this with Prometheus is using recording rules, but recording rules are going to be using the same query engine. So in reality, um you are fixing the latency issue for the user, but you are also moving all these queries and maybe we're going to be a single time adco queries. You're moving them and now you're going to be running them periodically and doing all the processing. So we wanted something that could just help um be more efficient in terms of how we first how we evaluate these queries that users are going to need and also how can we do it in a way that users don't need to be aware that they need to add recording rules.

They can just send the query and don't worry about it. Um so we had a few talks yesterday. Um Owen gave a great talk about the pros and cons of um delta temporality but tlddr we realize the same thing to be able to just aggregate. In this case, what I'm going to present works for any type of aggregations that you can parallelize because that's how scrapes run. Specifically, I'm going to be talking about adding up counters. And we realize that to be able to do that, you need deltas. And you can see very clearly here on the left side, you have a cumulative counter. You can have a huge value, millions, billions. You have a reset and goes all the way down to zero. But if you have deltas, you're going to have the gap because obviously you were not scraping anything during that time. But before that and after that you have this kind of steady value um that has a property that is additive.

So if we wanted to add up counters and just drop some labels you turn them into deltas you can add them up and the number is going to be correct. So we realize the same thing if we're going to be able to add up counters we need deltas but the problem with that is you cannot ingest or I didn't know maybe now you can ingest deltas in Prometheus and they have to be cumulative counters. So turning them into deltas is easy. How do you turn them back into cumulative counters in a way that is stateless is going to be the issue? Because as you add them up, the accumulative value that you're going to get changes depending on when you start counting. So if you have high availability, one replica can give you a very different value than the other just because they started at different times. So we fixed that using zigzags.

Um turns out zigzag is just a cumulative counter that you reset as soon as possible. You let it go up once and then you reset. And you can see why that works kind of visually here. It's kind of wrapping the delta. At the bottom we have a delta on top of a zigzag. It's just kind of wrapping the same the same shape. But the good thing is the one above it's a real cumulative counter you can just ingest in Prometheus and queries are going to are going to work fine. Rates are going to work fine. So that's how we fix the problem of make them deltas move them back to be cumulative counters send them to Prometheus and you can even dduplicate between these both replicas. So now um kind of spoiler of how it looks with what we have. We extended the this is on a Prometheus fork right now. We extended the Prometheus configuration and just added a new fields that we're going to use for these aggregations.

And I think the main ones are going to be flush interval. What we're going to be doing is that as we get these samples, um, we're going to aggregate them. We're going to keep them in memory and just flush them as if they were normal samples to the TSDB. Um, in in this case, we've been using 15 seconds to just kind of imitate what we have from scrapes. We have the stale time out. You don't want to keep this aggregation metrics forever if you're not getting any updates. So, after five minutes, which is our default, we just drop them. And then the main part is the aggregations is a list of multiples aggregations and the format follows the same thing you have for re label config. You have a source label separator rejects that you use to match the series that you're going to get and if they match that means that you're going to aggregate them.

And in this case the action is a type of aggregation um in increment without is just that we are going to add up these counters without rate. just add them up and drop the target labels and we're going to store them with a different name as if they were recording rules. And in this case, the suffix that we're using is just materialized. And you can see how it looks on the left side. You have your raw metric with instance and pot the classic infra labels. And then you have your materialized metrics without them. So how we did it was using a hook. You have your normal targets and scrapes. And every single time you scrape something, once that is committed and sent and stored in the TSDB, we also send these samples to the materialized metric store. And I'm going to talk about what the blue part looks like.

Um, but this was like the initial design. We send it to the materialized metric store. We are going to add up all the counters or just do any processing depending on the aggregation action. And periodically every 15 30 seconds, you're going to just flush them and send them to the TSV as if they were normal samples in a normal scrape. Um the challenge really is that you want that to work with everything else that you already have in Prometheus. You need the logs to work. Um you need to not block that logs from the other scrapes. Um you need the wall to work out of order. You need anything to work just as usual. So first where where is that aggregation going to live? And in my opinion, if I have a draft for a proposal and I think the start of that proposal is this aggregated head, um, aggregated head is just a new field and extension in the TSDB head.

It gets created every time Prometheus creates a new head, calls a new head method. Um, but the main the important point is that aggregated head is not the store. It doesn't have a wall. It doesn't have out of order. It doesn't have chunks. We just use it to create like a scratch path of the total value that we have. so far, which also means that after a restart, you just lose it. This is just what you've seen so far. And this is also the first version that we tried. Um, we're going to talk about the changes that that we needed to be able to have it ready for pro, but this is really like the first version that we had in code. It's just a mutx to make sure that you only one um only one thread is changing the head. And then we also have the aggregation series and some next ID as the TSDB. And this is how we did it.

We have the aggregated head that I just mentioned. As I said, everything is in memory. If permitious restarts, you lose everything. You don't need a wall. You don't need an and out of order. Then on the right side, we have the aggregation flush. It's a very very light implementation. So there's not much to say about that one. is just periodically you have a thicker and every 15 seconds 30 seconds you flush everything to a TSV as a normal sample happened and on the left side we have the aggate series which is the one that is going to be actually receiving the counters just checking if we need to aggregate these new series and then doing the actual delta back to cumulative conversion. So the left side is pretty uh pretty important. It was a real challenge because turns out that left side aggregate series is going to be in the hot spot in Prometheus.

It is something that is going to be running for every single target for every single sample that we get. Um and for each one of them we it's going to be running five different steps. The first one is get the labels of these new series. Apply the rejects and apply all the conditions that you have in your aggregations. Build the new labels and then hash them and see if you already have them in your allegation head. If you have them, add them up. If you don't have it created, that is a lot of work if you're going to do it for every single target and for every single sample. And you can probably notice that the first four steps, you don't need to do it every single time. Like your your configuration for materialized metrics is not really going to change that often compared to scrapes. And also your series are not going to change that often.

You're going to keep getting samples from the same series. You can of course get new ones, but most of them are going to be the same. So we improve this just by catching the first four steps. I get your labels u I have a cache of that to map your labels to the hash and I just have to do the fifth step. And that was really everything that we had to do for this part. Um that has been working. I'm going to show you some numbers at the end but that that has been working great for for the volume that we have. So now back to the um aggregation head which is the component at the middle. Um so when did the increments happen and how we are going to store this data in the first approach what we were using is as I said u this is a hook. So the time stamp that we get is when the scrape ended which is different from the default that you get in Prometheus in Prometheus the time stamp that you get in a sample is the time stamp when the scrape started.

Timing accuracy and production issues

So this is the first thing that we tried. We send this to the to the test cluster and basically you have all your data. You're not really losing any data. If you test this with a really long raid interval, let's say like an hour, you're going to see kind of the same values, but users are usually using great intervals of 1 minute, five minutes. And for those cases, the difference can be can be a lot of error margin. We were seeing up to 16.3% at some points. uh which is is it's bad if you want to use it for alerts that are using instant queries or you want to use it for SLOs's. So the first issue that we had is turns out using the commit time stamp instead of the the start of the scrape time stamp was a big big difference was a big issue. So fix that by using windows. Um you have your flush every 15 seconds but you also create a small windows uh which were implemented with a circular buffer and when you commit you also commit the start time stamp of the scrape and depending on on the time stamp you put it on different windows and this is going to this going to create two two things one accidental for us but that was also great.

Uh the first one, this is going to fix the issue with the difference between the start of the scrape time and end of the scrape time. But also since you're grouping these different scrapes, your in your time stamp is now going to be the start of the window. In this case, W and W + one instead of the scrape time stamp. And that is a that is a great improvement because now your intervals are going to be evenly distributed instead of just having all these multiple time stamps from the different scrapes that you are getting. So what these buys? Well, that really really help with the error margin. You can see uh yellow is the value you get from raw metrics and and green is the difference is the the error. I had to use these colors because otherwise the error margin was really really small. And this sends us from an error of 16.3% this is average error um to 2%.

And we can move that we can make it even lower. Um this is what we tested first in in with real production data. It worked great. We found multiple uh performance issues that we're going to talk um in the following slides. But I think this is a slide that follows. Yeah. If you have an instance ideal instance a feric instance that never fails. It never oops. It just works great. Um what I just showed you would would would just work. um we tested it with um I would say big enough instances with millions of cities and that was working great for months but then when we tried it in prod when we well we found all these issues that I'm going to mention now and and these are the ones that we really needed to fix to be able to run it with all the different shapes of Prometheuses that we have um yeah so the first one is late commits um obviously sometimes your window is going to close.

You're going to flush everything you have, but some of the scrapes are still going to be pending and running. So, an easy way of fixing that is what I have on the right side, which is just call them strugglers and send them to the next window. But that also means that the values that you're going to have in your samples is going to be different between the raw data and the materialized data, which is fine depending on your rate interval, but it's not something that we wanted. We wanted to be just as as as precise as possible. And the way we fix that is just moving the flush a little. Uh in this case, if you remember in the config, we had uh like a a flush weight time. And turns up just moving the flush for one second really fixed most of them. I would say it fixed about 90% of the strugglers that we had.

So now uh real time data is delayed by 1 second, but I would say we we haven't seen any issues with that. Um, and now if the scrape took longer than than that 1 second delay time, you can just send those stragglers to the same window so that when you look at the raw data, you're going to have a few samples with more like you're going to have a few a drop and then a little spike for your strugglers. Um, we also uh saw issues with flush stalls when you are compacting. If you don't have enough resources, you don't have CPU, you need more memory, something's going on. Sometimes uh Prometheus is going to delay flashing these um materialized metrics and as I said this is a circular buffer. So if you delay them for too long uh we need to reuse the oldest window and the way we fix that is since the goal is to not lose any data.

It is completely fine if data appears later but we do not want to lose any counts. we just reuse the window and add up the zoom value, the new one to the old one. So that some of the old data is going to appear now even though it was supposed to be 5 seconds, 15 seconds ago. Um that is better than losing it. So that's the way we fix that problem. And the other one, my favorite is batching. When I was working on this, I didn't think that flushing these materialist metrics was going to be an issue because technically in my mind, Prometheus is always scraping millions of series, millions of samples. So why would materialized metrics that in in order numbers at about 10% of metrics would be a problem and turns out it is a problem because when you have hundreds of targets um you can actually reuse the memory between them like you scrape once scrape ends and you can reuse that memory release and allocated something else.

So scraping uh flushing all these materialized metrics millions of them at the same time was an issue. We were blocking the the TSDB log for too long. So, we just fixed that with batching. Instead of doing all the millions at once, do a 100K at a time and that work fine. Finally, schedule. Um, I didn't know this, but turns out Prometheus isn't really scraping your targets exactly every 15 seconds. There's some jitter and it's just that if that jitter is small enough, it's going to tell you that it happened after 15 seconds. Um, I understand why that's necessary, but I didn't know that that was going on. So we had to do the same thing for materialized metrics to be able to compare the data raw data with the materialized metric data. We also had to implement this jitter for the flush interval.

You try to do it every 15 or the number that you configure. Uh but things happen if it was a few milliseconds before or after you just change that to make it look like it's happening exactly at the rate interval that you configure. And the last one was um retiring idle aggregates. You don't want to keep your materialized metrics forever. Some of these aggregations are not receiving any updates. I I played with this number. I was using one hour and then two hours because that's kind of the compaction um time which is what what you get when you're using Prometheus. You delete them when you compact. Uh but now we're using five minutes and it's working great. It wasn't really a resource problem. So being able to just remove all materialized metrics was another challenge that we had to fix in pro.

And finally the end results. Um this is a a real uh real test with broad data. We are flushing um 1.5 million subserious which is about 10% of everything all the counters that we have in this Prometheus of which about 1% is um stale serious and the other kind of 5% is strugglers. And you can see also the flusher ingestion lag. It is always 1 second because that is a L we're using to just to catch all the the um slow scrapes and we also have some spikes when we have compactions. That's the spike you're seeing there. Um yeah and uh I think that's it. Next step uh this is something as I said this was a first stage what we work on on on Reddit. It is definitely something that we want to send upstream. So I have a draft for a proposal ready that I'm going to be sending um probably in two weeks when I'm back in the US.

Um but yeah, I think that's it. Thank you.

aiSummary: Walther Lee 详解 Reddit 在采集阶段聚合 Prometheus 指标的方法，以及计数器转换、时间精度和生产故障修复。
oneSentenceSummary: Walther Lee 详解 Reddit 在采集阶段聚合 Prometheus 指标的方法，以及计数器转换、时间精度和生产故障修复。
summary: Walther Lee 介绍 Reddit 物化指标项目，重点展开摄取侧设计，并交代透明查询复用与 Thanos 集成的背景。实现将累计计数器转换为增量，去掉指定标签后聚合，再用快速复位的累计计数器表示结果，使已有查询能够继续计算 rate。内存聚合 head 和定期 flush 复用 TSDB 正常写入路径，缓存标签变换则减少热路径重复工作。生产测试发现，采用采集结束时间会影响短窗口计算；按采集开始时间划分窗口后，报告的平均误差从 16.3% 降至 2%。延迟 flush、分批写入、对齐抖动和回收闲置聚合分别处理迟到采集、锁占用和陈旧状态。讲者也讨论副本去重、重启和未来上游提案，强调这并不是能够运行任意录制规则的通用方案。

mainPoints.point: 在高成本查询之前完成可并行聚合
mainPoints.explanation: 采集时聚合减少反复扫描高基数原始序列，同时兼容现有面板与规则。

mainPoints.point: 计数器语义和时间对齐是基础
mainPoints.explanation: 增量转换、锯齿累计表示与时间窗口共同维持副本和不同采集时刻下的 rate 语义。

mainPoints.point: 生产可靠性取决于具体实现细节
mainPoints.explanation: 迟到等待、分批 flush、标签缓存、抖动对齐与闲置回收处理了真实故障和性能瓶颈。

keyQuotes: 因此我们用锯齿形式解决了这个问题。
我们持有 TSDB 锁的时间过长。
